q: What are platelets?

pts.a: Fragments (pieces) of cells, with no nucleus

right: Small fragments of cells that have no nucleus
wrong: Small white blood cells that make antibodies
Red blood cells that have lost their nucleus
Proteins dissolved in the plasma
why: Platelets are tiny fragments of cells. They have no nucleus, so they are not complete cells.

q: State the role of platelets in the blood.

pts.a: They help the blood to clot
accept: they form a clot at a cut

right: They help the blood to clot at a cut
wrong: They carry oxygen around the body
They make antibodies to fight infection
They carry dissolved food and hormones
why: At a cut, platelets stick together and release chemicals that turn the plasma protein fibrinogen into fibres of fibrin, which trap cells to form a clot.

q: Give two reasons why blood clotting is important.

accept: it stops you losing too much blood

pts.a: It stops germs (pathogens) getting into the body through the wound
accept: it keeps pathogens out of the body

right: It stops blood loss and stops germs entering the wound
wrong: It stops bleeding and carries oxygen to the wound
It makes antibodies and kills germs in the wound
It keeps blood pressure high and the heart beating
why: A clot seals the cut: it stops more blood being lost, and it forms a barrier so bacteria and other pathogens cannot get into the body.

q: Name the ABO blood group that can receive blood from donors of any ABO group.
right: Group AB, the universal recipient
wrong: Group O
Group A
Group B
why: Group AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so nothing in it attacks donated red cells of group A, B, AB or O.

q: Explain why blood of group O can be given to people of any ABO group.

pts.a: Its red blood cells have no A or B antigens, so the patient's antibodies do not attack them
accept: there are no antigens on group O red cells
O red cells lack the A and B antigens
the red cells carry neither the A nor the B antigen

right: Its red cells have no A or B antigens for antibodies to attack
wrong: Its plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies
Its red cells carry both the A and B antigens
It is the most common blood group in Ireland
why: Antibodies in a patient's plasma attack red cells that carry a foreign antigen. Group O red cells carry neither A nor B, so there is nothing to attack.

q: What is meant by saying that a person is Rhesus positive?

pts.a: The Rhesus (D) antigen is present on their red blood cells
accept: their red cells carry the Rhesus factor
they have the Rh antigen on their red blood cells
the Rhesus protein is on their red cells

right: Their red blood cells carry the Rhesus antigen
wrong: Their plasma contains anti-Rhesus antibodies
Their red cells carry both the A and B antigens
They can safely receive blood from any donor
why: Rhesus is a second blood-group system. Rhesus positive people have the Rhesus (D) antigen on their red cells; Rhesus negative people do not.

q: A Rhesus negative mother is carrying a Rhesus positive baby. What can her immune system make if some of the baby's blood enters her circulation?

pts.a: Antibodies against the Rhesus antigen (anti-Rhesus antibodies)
accept: antibodies against the baby's red blood cells

right: Antibodies against the Rhesus antigen (anti-Rhesus antibodies)
wrong: Rhesus antigens to coat her own red cells
Extra red blood cells to carry oxygen to the baby
Clotting proteins to stop the baby bleeding
why: Her immune system treats the Rhesus antigen on the baby's red cells as foreign, so it makes anti-Rhesus antibodies against it.

q: Explain how anti-Rhesus antibodies made by a Rhesus negative mother can harm a Rhesus positive baby in a later pregnancy.

pts.a: The antibodies cross the placenta into the baby's blood
accept: they get into the foetus's blood across the placenta

pts.a: They attack and destroy the baby's red blood cells (causing anaemia)
accept: they burst the baby's red cells
the baby's red blood cells are broken down
they make the baby's red cells clump

right: They cross the placenta and destroy the baby's red blood cells
wrong: They destroy the mother's own red blood cells
They stop oxygen crossing the placenta to the baby
They make the baby Rhesus negative like its mother
why: Antibodies are small enough to cross the placenta. In a Rhesus positive baby they attack its red cells, causing anaemia (Rhesus disease).

q: What happens to donated red blood cells if a patient is given blood of the wrong ABO group?

pts.a: The patient's antibodies attack them and they clump together (agglutinate)
accept: they are destroyed by the patient's antibodies

right: The patient's antibodies attack them, making them clump together
wrong: They change to match the patient's own blood group
They lose their haemoglobin and turn white
They pass into the tissue fluid and drain into lymph
why: Antibodies in the patient's plasma bind the foreign A or B antigens on the donor cells, so the cells clump (agglutinate) and burst, which can block vessels.

q: Name the substance that makes up about 90% of blood plasma.
right: Water, with other substances dissolved in it
wrong: Plasma proteins such as antibodies
Glucose and other dissolved food
Red blood cells
why: Plasma is about 90% water. Food, hormones, urea, carbon dioxide (as hydrogencarbonate) and plasma proteins are dissolved in it.

q: Give two functions of blood plasma.

pts.a: Transports dissolved food (e.g. glucose, amino acids)
Transports wastes such as urea and carbon dioxide (as hydrogencarbonate)
Carries the blood cells and platelets
Carries plasma proteins such as antibodies and clotting proteins

right: It carries dissolved food and hormones around the body
wrong: It carries oxygen on haemoglobin and engulfs germs
It makes red blood cells and kills bacteria
It carries dissolved food and engulfs bacteria
why: Plasma is the liquid that moves materials: dissolved food, hormones, wastes such as urea and CO2, plasma proteins and heat all travel in it.

q: Name a waste product made in the liver that is carried in the plasma to the kidneys.

accept: urea, from the breakdown of amino acids

right: Urea, made when excess amino acids are broken down
wrong: Glycogen
Bile
Carbon dioxide
why: The liver breaks down excess amino acids (deamination), making urea. It dissolves in the plasma and is carried to the kidneys to be excreted.

q: Explain how blood plasma helps to keep the temperature even throughout the body.

pts.a: It carries heat from warm, active organs (such as the liver and muscles) to cooler parts of the body
accept: it spreads heat around the body
it transports heat from the muscles and liver to the skin
it moves heat round the body

right: It carries heat from active organs like the liver to the rest of the body
wrong: Its proteins trap heat like a layer of fat under the skin
It makes the heart beat faster when the body is cold
It makes the skin sweat to cool the body down
why: Active organs such as the liver and muscles make heat. Plasma, which is mostly water, absorbs it and carries it round, spreading it through the body.

q: Which component of blood makes up about 55% of its volume?
right: Plasma, the liquid part of the blood
wrong: Red blood cells
White blood cells
Platelets
why: Plasma is about 55% of blood. The other 45% is almost all red blood cells; white cells and platelets make up less than 1%.

q: Name two components of blood other than plasma.
right: Red blood cells and platelets
wrong: Water and dissolved glucose
Haemoglobin and antibodies
Lymph and tissue fluid
why: Blood is plasma plus three solid parts: red blood cells to carry oxygen, white blood cells to fight infection, and platelets to help it clot.

q: Which type of blood cell is the most numerous in the blood?
right: Red blood cells
wrong: White blood cells
Lymphocytes
Platelets
why: There are about 5 million red cells in each cubic millimetre of blood, against only a few thousand white cells, so almost all blood cells are red.

q: Explain how phagocytes (monocytes) protect the body against infection.

pts.a: They engulf (surround and take in) pathogens and digest them
accept: they surround germs and destroy them

right: They engulf germs and digest them with enzymes
wrong: They make antibodies that stick to germs
They help the blood to clot at a cut
They carry oxygen to infected cells
why: Phagocytes change shape to surround a pathogen and take it in, then digest it with enzymes. Lymphocytes, not phagocytes, make antibodies.

q: Name the type of white blood cell that makes antibodies.
right: Lymphocytes
wrong: Monocytes
Platelets
Red blood cells
why: B lymphocytes make antibodies that fit a particular antigen on a pathogen. Monocytes (phagocytes) engulf pathogens instead.

q: Blood enters the heart from the vena cava. Name the chamber it enters and the valve it then passes through.
right: The right atrium, then the tricuspid valve
wrong: The left atrium, then the bicuspid valve
The right ventricle, then a semilunar valve
The right atrium, then a semilunar valve
why: Deoxygenated blood from the body comes in through the vena cava to the right atrium, then passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

q: Blood enters the heart from the pulmonary vein. Name the chamber it enters and the valve it then passes through.
right: The left atrium, then the bicuspid valve
wrong: The right atrium, then the tricuspid valve
The left ventricle, then a semilunar valve
The right ventricle, then the bicuspid valve
why: The pulmonary vein empties into the left atrium. When the atrium contracts, blood is pushed through the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle.

q: Deoxygenated blood leaves a kidney. Name the two blood vessels it flows through to get back to the heart.
right: The renal vein, then the vena cava
wrong: The renal artery, then the aorta
The renal vein, then the pulmonary vein
The ureter, then the vena cava
why: The renal vein drains each kidney into the inferior vena cava, which carries the deoxygenated blood back to the right atrium.

q: Blood leaves the right ventricle. Name the vessel it is pumped into and the organ this vessel carries it to.
right: The pulmonary artery, which takes it to the lungs
wrong: The aorta, which takes it round the body
The pulmonary vein, which takes it to the lungs
The vena cava, which takes it to the liver
why: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood past a semilunar valve into the pulmonary artery, which takes it to the lungs to pick up oxygen.

q: What name is given to the death of part of the heart muscle when a coronary artery becomes blocked?
right: A heart attack (myocardial infarction)
wrong: A stroke
Angina
A heart murmur
why: If a coronary artery is blocked, the heart muscle it supplies gets no oxygen and dies. This is a heart attack, or myocardial infarction.

q: Explain why heart muscle cells die if the coronary artery supplying them is completely blocked.

pts.a: No blood reaches them, so they get no oxygen (or glucose)
accept: the cells get no oxygen or glucose
there is a lack of oxygen

pts.a: They cannot carry out (aerobic) respiration, so they have no energy (ATP)
accept: they have no energy to contract

right: No oxygen reaches them, so they cannot respire to release energy
wrong: No blood reaches the lungs, so the body gets no oxygen
The heart valves stop closing, so blood flows backwards
Too much carbon dioxide reaches the cells and poisons them
why: The coronary arteries are the heart muscle's own blood supply. Blocked, they bring no oxygen or glucose, so the cells cannot respire, run out of energy and die.

q: A blood pressure trace shows one heartbeat every 0.8 seconds. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
right: 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 beats per minute
wrong: 0.8 × 60 = 48 beats per minute
60 ÷ 8 = 7.5 beats per minute
0.8 ÷ 60 = 0.013 beats per minute
why: Heart rate is beats per minute, so divide the 60 seconds in a minute by the time for one beat: 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 beats per minute.

q: A blood pressure trace shows the heart beating 5 times in 3 seconds. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
right: 5 × (60 ÷ 3) = 5 × 20 = 100 beats per minute
wrong: 5 × 3 = 15 beats per minute
60 ÷ 5 × 3 = 36 beats per minute
5 × 60 = 300 beats per minute
why: A minute holds 20 lots of 3 seconds (60 ÷ 3 = 20), so the heart beats 5 × 20 = 100 times a minute. Or: one beat takes 0.6 s, and 60 ÷ 0.6 = 100.
